--- title: Talking to machines 🤖 subtitle: Learn how to use Large Language Models programmatically with ellmer author: "Nelson Amaya" description: "LLMs are not just chatbots: they are functions you can call from R. Learn to chat, design prompts, extract structured data from text, and give models tools --all with ellmer." categories: - LLM - ellmer - AI - structured data - API date: "2026-07-04" date-modified: last-modified image: robot.gif editor_options: chunk_output_type: console aliases: - /sessions_workshop/09-llm/09-llm.html citation: url: https://r4dev.netlify.app/sessions_ai/01-llm/01-llm --- > *"The question of whether a computer can think is no more interesting than the question of whether a submarine can swim."*
--Edsger W. Dijkstra ## PART I: An LLM is a function You have used a chatbot. This session is about something more useful: calling a Large Language Model **from code**, where its answers become objects you can filter, join, plot and disagree with --like any other data. The package for this in R is [**`ellmer`**](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/), from the tidyverse team. It speaks to every major provider --Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, local models via [Ollama](https://ollama.com/)-- with the same functions, so nothing you learn today is tied to one company. ::: callout-tip ## Get a key, keep it secret This workshop's default is **Google Gemini**, because its [free tier](https://aistudio.google.com/apikey) requires no credit card: create a key in two minutes. Then store it where R finds it and **no one else does** --your `.Renviron` file, *never* your script: ``` r usethis::edit_r_environ() # opens .Renviron; add the line below and restart R # GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key-here ``` Remember session 2: this workshop once leaked a pair of Spotify credentials by writing them in a script. Learn from our sins. ::: Every conversation starts by creating a **chat object**, and the `system prompt` is where you tell the model who it should be: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini( # <1> system_prompt = "You are a terse assistant embedded in an R data-analysis workshop. One short paragraph max." # <2> ) chat$chat("In one sentence: what is a Large Language Model, really?") # <3> ``` ::: ``` #> An LLM is a neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the #> next word in a sequence, which when repeated millions of times produces #> human-like language output. ``` 1. The `chat_*()` family picks your provider: `chat_google_gemini()`, `chat_anthropic()`, `chat_openai()`, `chat_ollama()`... swap this one line and everything else in this session works unchanged. 2. The **system prompt** sets behaviour for the whole conversation --tone, format, role, constraints. It is the single highest-leverage sentence you will write. 3. `$chat()` sends a message and returns the answer as a plain string. The `$` syntax is new: chat objects are [R6 objects](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/r6.html), little machines that carry their own state --the conversation history. The system prompt is not decoration. Watch it completely change the machine: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poet <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini( system_prompt = "You answer strictly in haiku. Never break form." ) poet$chat("Why should economists learn R?") ``` ::: ``` #> Data speaks true here, #> R unlocks hidden patterns— #> Economics grows. ``` ::: callout-important ## Same question, different answers Model outputs on this page were captured once (with Claude Haiku) and pasted in --run the code and **your answers will differ**, even between two identical runs. LLMs are *stochastic*: they sample from a probability distribution over words. Treat every output the way you would treat a colleague's first draft: plausible, useful, and unverified. ::: ## PART II: From prose to tibbles Chatting is a party trick. The feature that changes your work as an analyst is **structured extraction**: you describe the shape of the data you want --a `type_object()`, like a contract-- and `ellmer` forces the model's answer into exactly that shape. Text goes in, a tibble comes out. Remember the Kyoto cherry blossoms from session 2? Here is a news-style paragraph about them, the kind of unstructured text the world produces by the ton: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) passage <- "The 2024 cherry blossom season in Kyoto reached full bloom on April 4th, five days earlier than the 20th-century average. Tokyo peaked on April 6th, while Sapporo, far to the north, waited until May 1st. Experts attribute the shift to a March that averaged 2.1 degrees Celsius above the historical norm." bloom_type <- type_array( # <4> type_object( # <4> city = type_string("Name of the city"), # <5> full_bloom = type_string("Date of full bloom, ISO format, assume 2024"), # <5> note = type_string("Any qualifier the text attaches to this city, or empty") # <5> ) ) extractor <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini() extractor$chat_structured( # <6> paste("Extract every city mentioned with its full-bloom date:", passage), type = bloom_type ) ``` ::: ``` #> # A tibble: 3 × 3 #> city full_bloom note #> #> 1 Kyoto 2024-04-04 "five days earlier than the 20th-century average" #> 2 Tokyo 2024-04-06 "" #> 3 Sapporo 2024-05-01 "far to the north" ``` 4. `type_array()` of `type_object()`s means "I want a table with these columns" --one object per row. 5. Each field gets a *description*, which is really a mini-prompt: the model reads it to decide what goes in the column. Notice how `"ISO format, assume 2024"` quietly handles the date parsing that would take you three lines of `lubridate`. 6. `$chat_structured()` is `$chat()` with a contract attached. The answer is not prose --it is data, ready for `ggplot`. Think about what just happened: **the PDF scraping, regex wrangling and date parsing of session 3 collapsed into a schema and one function call.** Not always this cleanly --but this is now a tool in your box, and it works on interview transcripts, policy documents, survey open-ends, 19th-century books... ### The machine judges our music Let's do extraction *at scale*, and be properly skeptical about it. From session 2's Spotify archive we sampled 48 songs. We asked the model to rate --**judging only by the title**-- how positive each song sounds, using `parallel_chat_structured()` to score them all concurrently: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ellmer) songs <- readr::read_csv(paste0(getwd(), "/llm_mood_scores.csv")) |> # <7> dplyr::select(-llm_mood) mood_type <- type_object( mood = type_number("How positive/happy this song title sounds, 0 = bleak, 1 = euphoric") ) prompts <- ellmer::interpolate( # <8> "Judging ONLY by its title, how positive does the song '{{songs$track_name}}' by {{songs$artist}} sound?" ) scorer <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini() moods <- ellmer::parallel_chat_structured(scorer, as.list(prompts), type = mood_type) # <9> songs$llm_mood <- moods$mood ``` ::: 7. The song sample ships with this session --and so do the scores we got, so the next chunk runs without any API key. 8. `interpolate()` builds one prompt per row from a template, `glue`-style. Templates keep your prompts out of `paste()` spaghetti. 9. `parallel_chat_structured()` sends all 48 prompts concurrently and returns one tidy data frame. Scoring cost about half a cent. Now the real question: does the machine's guess agree with Spotify's `valence`, which was computed from the *audio itself*? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ggrepel) mood_scores <- readr::read_csv(paste0(getwd(), "/llm_mood_scores.csv")) mood_scores |> ggplot(aes(x = valence, y = llm_mood)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") + # <10> geom_point(aes(color = artist), size = 2, show.legend = FALSE) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( # <11> data = \(d) dplyr::slice_max(d, abs(valence - llm_mood), n = 4), # <11> aes(label = track_name), size = 3, color = "grey30" ) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs( title = "Judging songs by their covers", subtitle = paste0("Correlation: ", round(cor(mood_scores$valence, mood_scores$llm_mood), 2), " — song titles carry almost no information about how the music feels"), x = "Spotify valence (from the audio)", y = "LLM mood score (from the title alone)" ) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The LLM never heard the song](01-llm_files/figure-html/9.mood-plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 10. The dashed line is perfect agreement. Look how far we are from it. 11. We label the biggest disagreements --`slice_max()` inside a layer's `data` argument is a neat trick for annotating outliers only. The correlation is **essentially zero**. The model did exactly what we asked --it judged titles, competently-- and what we asked was not informative. Hold on to this lesson: *an articulate answer is not evidence that the question was answerable.* The most dangerous LLM failure is not a wrong answer; it is a confident answer to a question the input cannot support. ## PART III: Give the machine your tools One more superpower. An LLM knows nothing about *right now* --its training data ended months ago. But you can hand it **your R functions** and let it decide when to call them. Here we wrap the Open-Meteo API from session 2 into a function, register it, and ask a question the model cannot answer alone: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) weather_now <- function(latitude, longitude) { # <12> httr2::request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |> httr2::req_url_query(latitude = latitude, longitude = longitude, current = "temperature_2m") |> httr2::req_perform() |> httr2::resp_body_json() |> purrr::pluck("current", "temperature_2m") } assistant <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini() assistant$register_tool(tool( # <13> weather_now, "Gets the current temperature in Celsius at a location", arguments = list( latitude = type_number("Latitude in decimal degrees"), longitude = type_number("Longitude in decimal degrees") ) )) assistant$chat("Is it warmer right now in Kyoto or in Paris? Answer in one sentence with the temperatures.") # <14> ``` ::: ``` #> Kyoto is warmer right now at 23.3°C compared to Paris at 16.8°C. ``` 12. An ordinary R function --nothing special about it. Yours could query your database, run a model, read a file. 13. `register_tool()` describes the function to the model: what it does, what arguments it takes. The descriptions are prompts --write them like documentation. 14. Watch the loop: the model reads the question, decides it needs data, calls `weather_now()` **twice** (once per city, working out the coordinates itself), reads the numbers, and composes the answer. That loop --model, tools, model again-- is what people mean by the word **agent**. ::: callout-tip ## What this costs, roughly Providers charge per **token** (~¾ of a word). Everything executed while writing this session --every example, including scoring 48 songs-- cost **under two US cents** on a small model. The free Gemini tier covers the whole session comfortably. Big models for hard problems, small models for bulk work: choosing the right size is a real skill. ::: ## 🏗 Practice 9: Talk back {.unnumbered} ::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"} # Easy - Create a chat object with a system prompt that makes the model answer like a pirate, and ask it about the tidyverse - Change the system prompt to "Answer only with valid R code, no prose" and ask it to plot `diamonds`. Run what it returns. Would you have written it the same way? ::: ::: {.callout-important icon="false" collapse="true"} # Intermediate - Take three paragraphs from any news article and design a `type_object()` that extracts *who did what, where, when*. Where does the model struggle? - Re-run the mood-scoring experiment, but give the model the **lyrics' first line** instead of the title (scrape them --session 6 taught you how). Does the correlation with valence improve? ::: ::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"} # Advanced - Register two tools --`weather_now()` and a function that geocodes a city name using the [Open-Meteo geocoding API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/geocoding-api)-- and ask for the temperature in five cities without ever typing a coordinate :::
